title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Manufacturing
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Clop names more than 40 PTC Windchill victims and what it took is your engineering record
items.content_text: The Clop extortion group has listed over 40 organisations on its leak site after a mass data-theft campaign against internet-exposed PTC Windchill and FlexPLM product lifecycle management platforms, exploiting CVE-2026-12569, an improper input validation flaw allowing arbitrary code execution. Named organisations include Shell, Philips, Fiserv, Zebra, Mindray and Largan Precision. Researchers report affiliates deploying JSP web shells to exfiltrate data, with confirmed victims across manufacturing, automotive, aerospace and retail, and activity running since early June. What was taken is specific to this sector: engineering blueprints, product designs and manufacturing specifications. That is the material a competitor wants and the material that makes a later targeted intrusion into your plant substantially cheaper, because it hands over your process, your tolerances and often your control system architecture in one archive.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Clop leak-site listings — reported by SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Listings reported 15 Aug 2026; campaign since early Jun 2026

items.title: Treasury names an Iranian intelligence-directed hacking network operating inside US critical infrastructure
items.content_text: The US Treasury designated an Iranian Ministry of Intelligence and Security–directed hacking group on 24 August, within a wider action covering nearly 60 Iran-linked people, entities and vessels. Five alleged operators, described as tied to the Mabna Institute, were indicted by the Justice Department the preceding week. Treasury says the network has been breaching and exfiltrating data from US energy companies, defence contractors, healthcare providers, IT firms and banks since at least late 2023. The scope is worth reading precisely: what is attributed here is espionage and data theft, not manipulation of process equipment. The State Department has posted a $10 million reward on related activity. Manufacturers should map the named victim set onto their own position rather than dismiss it as an energy-sector story. Defence contractors and IT service firms are explicitly listed, which puts tier-one and tier-two suppliers, contract manufacturers and the integrators who hold your project files inside the described target space. What this cluster is accused of taking — design documentation, network diagrams, credentials and personnel records — is the same category of material Clop has been exfiltrating from internet-exposed PLM platforms this month, and the reason is the same: engineering data is durable, sellable and useful for the next intrusion. The operational point is that credentials and vendor footholds collected for espionage are inherited intact by whoever is tasked next.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: US Treasury press release and OFAC designations; Department of Justice indictment; State Department Rewards for Justice notice — via The Hacker News, CyberScoop and Nextgov/FCW
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Designations announced 24 Aug 2026; DOJ indictments the preceding week; trade-press analysis 25 Aug 2026

items.title: A small UK generator lost four days to a cyberattack — and plant-site self-generation sits in exactly that blind spot
items.content_text: The Sunday Telegraph reported on 22 August that Iran-linked hackers took a British power plant offline for four days. The UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has since confirmed on the record that an incident occurred at a small-scale energy generator, and that the wider energy system was never at risk; the four-day outage, the attribution to Iran and the “unprecedented” label remain Telegraph sourcing that the NCSC would not comment on. The reason it belongs on a manufacturing page is the detail underneath: the NCSC is understood to have logged no outage reports from regulated power station operators, meaning the affected generator sat below the regulated reporting threshold. That describes a very large amount of industrial infrastructure. On-site CHP, cogeneration and steam plant, standby and peaking generators, plant battery storage and behind-the-meter renewables are generating assets that manufacturers own, that fall outside energy-sector regulation, and that are almost always commissioned and remotely supported by the OEM or an integrator rather than run by the site’s own controls team. They frequently sit on their own PLC and HMI stack, reached over a vendor VPN or a cellular router that never appears in the plant network diagram. A four-day loss of one of those assets is not a grid event — it is a production event, and it is yours. Read alongside AA26-231A naming Siemens S7 controllers an active target across critical manufacturing, the pattern is consistent: pressure is landing on the reachable, lightly-governed edge of the plant.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Sunday Telegraph report, with on-record statement from the UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero — via Irish Times, CNBC, Security Affairs
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Telegraph report 22 Aug 2026; DESNZ statement 23 Aug 2026; attack reported as occurring in July 2026, exact date not published

items.title: A chip-programming supplier pulled its own production and shipping systems offline to contain ransomware — and told the SEC it has no restoration date
items.content_text: Data I/O Corporation, a Washington-state manufacturer whose semiconductor programming systems are used by automotive, industrial and consumer electronics makers, disclosed ransomware in a Form 8-K filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on 21 August. The company detected the intrusion on 16 August and, as a containment measure, took systems offline itself — including internal communications, shipping, receiving, manufacturing production and other support functions. The filing states the company has not been able to estimate when normal operations will resume and that the financial impact cannot yet be determined. This is the recurring pattern in industrial ransomware: the attacker never had to touch a PLC. Losing ERP, shipping and production scheduling stops output just as effectively, and the decision to disconnect was the operator’s own.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Data I/O Corporation Form 8-K filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission — reported by The Record, CyberScoop and SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Ransomware detected 16 Aug 2026; 8-K filed and disruption confirmed 21 Aug 2026

items.title: Five federal agencies warn AI-written scripts are reading Siemens S7 controllers, critical manufacturing named first
items.content_text: The NSA, CISA, FBI, Department of Energy and EPA issued a joint advisory on 19 August warning that threat actors are combining the open-source snap7 and python-snap7 automation libraries with AI-assisted scripting to build custom tools that mimic legitimate OT monitoring solutions. Those tools provide read and write access to Siemens S7 controller memory, configuration data and ladder logic programs over S7comm. Critical manufacturing is named first among the most-targeted sectors, ahead of energy, water, chemical, food and agriculture, and commercial facilities. The agencies state that this is an active threat rather than a theoretical one, and that AI-generated exploitation scripts dramatically reduce the expertise and time needed. Actors find exposed or poorly segmented devices with internet scanning services and gain access through default or weakly configured credentials. Affected lines span S7-200, S7-300 including 314, 315 and 317, S7-400, S7-1200 CPUs 1211C through 1217C, and S7-1500 including F-series safety controllers. The agencies assess current activity as reconnaissance and capability development, with read access used to prepare for later write operations.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Joint advisory AA26-231A (NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE, EPA) — corroborated by SecurityWeek and Help Net Security

items.title: Attackers crossed from a wind farm into an unrelated plant over a shared private cellular APN
items.content_text: CERT Polska disclosed on 9 August that attackers reached the industrial control network of a Polish combined heat and power plant serving roughly 50,000 residents by pivoting through a private cellular data network. The intrusion started at an entirely different organisation: an internet-exposed Fortinet VPN and firewall device at a wind farm sharing the same carrier APN. Because the APN was misconfigured to allow arbitrary devices to communicate with one another, the attacker crossed from one operator’s network into another’s controllers. CERT Polska describes this as the first observed real-world use of a private APN as an OT attack vector. The incident occurred on 29 December 2025 and analysis took over three months. The relevance to manufacturers is architectural: private APN and private 5G are being sold into plants for machine connectivity and remote-site telemetry on the premise that they are safer than the public internet, and a flat one is a shared broadcast domain with other subscribers.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CERT Polska disclosure — reported by SecurityWeek, Help Net Security and BleepingComputer
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Incident 29 Dec 2025; disclosed 9 Aug 2026, analysis published 10–11 Aug 2026

items.title: CISA’s red team took a domain undetected — the tooling was fine, the monitoring was not
items.content_text: CISA published AA26-237A on 25 August comparing two red-team assessments run with near-identical tradecraft: one against a government services and facilities organisation, one against a water and wastewater systems entity. Both opened with phishing and escalated through Active Directory weaknesses that are ordinary rather than exotic — a Machine Account Quota left at its default of 10, and misconfigured Active Directory Certificate Services templates. The outcomes diverged sharply. At the organisation CISA labels A, the team obtained elevated domain privileges and reached sensitive business systems and cloud resources without ever being detected, despite the organisation running multiple security operations centres and multiple EDR products. CISA’s stated reason deserves reading twice: the SOCs did not communicate with one another, and thousands of false positives from routine business activity buried the real signal. For a manufacturer the relevance is direct and uncomfortable. Engineering workstations, historian servers and MES application hosts are almost always joined to the corporate Active Directory that this tradecraft targets, which means a domain compromise is one trust relationship away from the production estate. Both weaknesses CISA names cost nothing to fix. The detection finding is the one to take to a plant leadership meeting: having more tooling did not help, because nobody was correlating across consoles and routine business noise buried the signal — a familiar shape in multi-site manufacturers where each plant, and often each acquisition, brought its own monitoring arrangement.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA cybersecurity advisory AA26-237A — joint red-team assessment findings

items.title: Manufacturing took 747 of 1,140 industrial ransomware incidents in the second quarter
items.content_text: Dragos recorded 1,140 ransomware incidents involving industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up 12 percent from 1,020 in the first. Manufacturing accounted for 747 of them, roughly 65 percent of the total, with construction at 176, equipment manufacturing at 114 and food and beverage at 70. The analytical point matters more than the count: ransomware operators do not need control system access to disrupt industrial production, because encrypting the IT systems that support the plant — scheduling, planning, shipping, quality records — is regularly sufficient to stop the line. Extortion also continued its shift away from file encryption toward data theft, which changes the calculus around backups. A plant that can restore every server in eight hours has not addressed the leverage created by an attacker who took the design files and never encrypted anything.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Dragos Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis — via Help Net Security

items.title: A conferencing server was made to hand out a backdoored client to the engineers who joined the call
items.content_text: Kaspersky ICS-CERT reported on 12 August that the Head Mare group chained two flaws in unpatched TrueConf Server installations — tracked by Kaspersky as KLCERT-26-057 and KLCERT-26-058 — to run code and escalate privileges on the server, then swapped the legitimate client installer for a trojanised build carrying the PhantomCore and PhantomGraph backdoors. Anyone who subsequently updated their conferencing client from that server was infected. The victims named span instrumentation, electronics, transportation, energy, IT and software development. TrueConf shipped fixes on 18 June 2026 for versions 5.3.x before 5.3.9, 5.4.x before 5.4.9 and 5.5.x before 5.5.5; the exploited servers were simply never updated. Instrumentation and electronics firms are explicitly named among the victims, which puts this squarely in the discrete and process manufacturing space. Engineering workstations are the crown jewels of a plant network — they hold PLC project files, HMI runtimes and vendor remote-support tooling — and they belong to precisely the staff most likely to be running a conferencing client that self-updates from a corporate server.

items.title: CISA sets a three-day federal deadline on a CVSS 10.0 Oracle web-tier flaw now under active attack
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-21962 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 24 August with a remediation date of 27 August — the tightest window Binding Operational Directive 26-04 permits. The flaw is an improper access control issue in Oracle HTTP Server and in the Oracle WebLogic Server Proxy Plug-in for Apache HTTP Server and Microsoft IIS, scored CVSS 10.0. It is reachable over HTTP by an unauthenticated attacker with no user interaction and no existing privileges, and successful exploitation allows access to the instance or modification of the data it fronts. Oracle shipped the fix in its January 2026 critical patch update; reporting on 25 August describes broad exploitation against WebLogic servers. A three-day federal deadline is the signal worth reading — CISA reserves that window for exploitation it judges both live and consequential. This is not an ICS product and it will not sit on the plant floor, but Oracle’s web tier is a very common reverse proxy in front of the business systems that keep production moving: ERP and MES web front-ends, supplier and customer portals, quality and document management, and the reporting layers that pull from the historian. Dragos’ second-quarter analysis made the point that industrial production stops without anyone writing to a controller — ERP, scheduling and identity are enough. This is exactly that class of exposure, now with confirmed exploitation and a three-day federal clock.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition; Oracle critical patch update — corroborated by SecurityWeek and The Hacker News
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Added to KEV 24 Aug 2026; federal remediation deadline 27 Aug 2026; Oracle fix issued Jan 2026; broad exploitation reported 25 Aug 2026

items.title: Citrix is telling admins to patch NetScaler now — an unauthenticated bypass on the appliance that fronts most OT remote access
items.content_text: Citrix published bulletin CTX696939 on 20 August covering two NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway flaws. The serious one, CVE-2026-19490, is an authentication bypass carrying a CVSS score of 9.3: on Gateway and AAA virtual-server configurations an unauthenticated attacker can skip the login step entirely. The second, CVE-2026-19489, is a memory overflow that can produce unpredictable behaviour or a denial of service, and only applies where SIP ALG is enabled on a Large Scale NAT group. Fixed builds are 14.1-73.32 and 13.1-63.21 or later. Citrix, Rapid7 and Finland’s national cyber authority all said they were not aware of in-the-wild exploitation at publication, while urging immediate patching — NetScaler has a long record of exploited edge flaws. In manufacturing this is the appliance that carries OEM and integrator access into engineering workstations, MES and line-control networks — the same access path that keeps a machine builder able to dial in at 2am. An unauthenticated bypass on it removes the one control most plants are relying on to keep that path safe.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Citrix security bulletin CTX696939 — reported by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News

items.title: Fire-alarm management software stores its credentials in cleartext in memory, CISA warns
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-232-01 on 20 August covering Johnson Controls Simplex Incident Manager, the software operators use to monitor and manage Simplex fire alarm panels across a property portfolio. Versions up to and including V2.01 keep user passwords and authentication tokens unencrypted in system memory while the application runs, tracked as CVE-2026-27875 and classified as CWE-316. A local attacker who already holds low-privileged access to the workstation can read those credentials out of memory and reuse them against the application and the systems it connects to. CISA lists critical manufacturing, commercial facilities, government facilities, transportation systems and energy among the affected sectors, with deployment worldwide. Johnson Controls has published remediation guidance in JCI-PSA-2026-28. CISA lists critical manufacturing first among the affected sectors. Plants run Simplex fire detection across production halls and warehousing, and the management workstation usually lives with facilities on the business network — shared login, physically accessible, rarely inventoried by the OT team. That is the foothold this flaw converts into working credentials.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-232-01; Johnson Controls product security advisory JCI-PSA-2026-28

items.title: August ICS Patch Tuesday: maximum-severity missing authentication in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced
items.content_text: Siemens published ten advisories in the August cycle. The most serious, SSA-834709, covers a maximum-severity missing authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices allowing a remote, unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the underlying server with elevated privileges. Siemens also fixed a critical code execution vulnerability in Siveillance Video Management Servers, and high-severity flaws in Solid Edge, Simcenter Nastran, Siemens License Server, Simcenter Femap, Parasolid and Logo! Soft Comfort that can crash applications, execute arbitrary code, elevate privileges, read arbitrary files or leak information. Medium-severity issues were resolved in Ruggedcom devices and Desigo controllers. Schneider Electric published advisories for NetBotz 5 and PowerChute Serial Shutdown, and Phoenix Contact issued one covering multiple PLCnext firmware flaws. Several of the Siemens items are engineering-workstation software rather than plant devices — Solid Edge, Femap, Nastran and Parasolid all run on the machines that also hold your TIA Portal projects.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Siemens ProductCERT SSA-834709, Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact advisories — summarised by SecurityWeek

items.title: Cisco ASA and FTD VPN zero-day exploited to reload firewalls, added to CISA KEV
items.content_text: Cisco has patched CVE-2026-20349, a flaw in the remote-access SSL VPN service of Secure Firewall ASA and Secure Firewall Threat Defense software that attackers are exploiting to force appliances offline. A specially crafted HTTP request causes an unexpected reload and a denial-of-service condition, with no authentication and no user interaction required. Cisco’s PSIRT confirmed active exploitation in August and CISA added the flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue with a federal remediation deadline of 14 August. Hot fixes cover ASA 9.16, 9.18, 9.20, 9.22, 9.23 and 9.24 and FTD 7.0, 7.2, 7.4, 7.6, 7.7 and 10.0. For manufacturers the operational risk is loss of remote support at the wrong moment: these appliances usually terminate machine-builder and integrator access into the plant, and a line down at 2am with the OEM unable to connect is a longer outage than the firewall reload itself suggests.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Cisco security advisory and CISA KEV catalogue — reported by Help Net Security and SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Exploitation confirmed and KEV listed Aug 2026; reported 13 Aug 2026

items.title: Four more exploited flaws added to KEV on 18 August, including Windows IKE and VMware vCenter
items.content_text: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 August: CVE-2026-33824 in Microsoft Internet Key Exchange, CVE-2026-55040 in Microsoft SharePoint, CVE-2026-59310 in Broadcom VMware vCenter and CVE-2026-65400 in Apple macOS. Two further additions followed on 20 August, both in TrueConf Server. For manufacturers, vCenter is the one that changes the risk model: it commonly manages the virtual infrastructure hosting MES, historians, SCADA servers and virtualised engineering workstations, so a compromise there is a hypervisor problem affecting every OT workload on the cluster at once, not an application problem. IKE terminates site-to-site tunnels between plants, to corporate, and to machine builders. SharePoint deserves a second look because standard operating procedures, machine manuals and process documentation are so often stored there and treated as low-sensitivity.

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Added 18 Aug 2026; two further additions 20 Aug 2026

items.title: CISA publishes an advisory for flaws in Malcolm, its own free OT monitoring suite
items.content_text: Advisory ICSA-26-230-01 covers vulnerabilities in Malcolm, the network traffic analysis suite CISA distributes free for OT and ICS environments, which could allow an attacker to cause a denial-of-service condition or execute arbitrary code. Affected versions are below 26.06.1, below 26.07.0 and up to and including 26.07.1. The same day CISA published ICSA-26-230-02 covering a stack overflow in Siemens Simcenter Nastran that can be triggered when the application binary reads an arbitrary string as a file argument, with remote code execution possible if a user is tricked into running it; Siemens has released updated versions. Malcolm shows up in manufacturing more often than its profile suggests, usually as a pilot a controls engineer or a consultant stood up to demonstrate network visibility before a budget request — sitting on a span port with sight of the whole plant network, and almost never in a patch inventory.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-230-01 and ICSA-26-230-02

items.title: AVEVA Enterprise SCADA can be pushed into executing code through tampered serialised data
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-01, published 13 August as part of a 15-advisory batch, covers a deserialisation flaw in AVEVA Enterprise SCADA. An attacker who already holds the “DNA Authority — Operator” privilege can tamper with serialised data and have it execute as code when the server deserialises it. The 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 release families are affected, along with certain Enterprise SCADA HMI versions. CISA reports no known public exploitation targeting this flaw. AVEVA’s guidance is to restrict operator rights to trusted users, disallow BLT test clients in production, and audit devices, network topology and perimeter defences; the vendor also points to KB117814 on removing the binary formatter. Enterprise SCADA sits above the line-level controls in process plants and across multi-site operations, which makes it a high-value pivot: code execution on the SCADA server puts an attacker in the same trust zone as the historians, alarm servers and the operator HMIs. The operator-privilege requirement is real mitigation, but shared control-room logins erode it quickly.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICSA-26-225-01 — corroborated by AVEVA security bulletin AVEVA-2026-005

items.title: From 11 September 2026 manufacturers must report exploited vulnerabilities within 24 hours
items.content_text: The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s reporting obligations take effect on 11 September 2026. From that date, manufacturers of products with digital elements placed on the EU market must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents affecting the security of those products. The timelines are tight: an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware, a full notification within 72 hours, and a final report within 14 days of a corrective measure being available for an actively exploited vulnerability, or within a month for a severe incident. Reporting goes through a single reporting platform to the relevant national CSIRT, with information made available to ENISA at the same time. Two points are routinely missed. The obligations cover products already on the EU market, not just new launches, so legacy product lines are in scope. And if your machines, controllers or embedded software reach EU customers, you are the manufacturer here — this is not only a supplier concern.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: European Commission, Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations

items.title: US and Australian agencies publish guidance on isolating OT and running that way for an extended period
items.content_text: A joint publication from US and Australian agencies sets out how critical infrastructure operators should prepare to isolate vital operational technology and supporting systems from external connectivity, and to keep operating in that isolated state for an extended period rather than the few hours most continuity plans assume. It is guidance and creates no obligation. Its value for a manufacturer is that it converts a claim most plants make confidently — that the line can keep running if corporate is compromised — into a dependency checklist. The items that break first are rarely on the network diagram as control-system dependencies: time synchronisation, Active Directory authentication for HMI logins, licence servers for HMI and historian software, MES order release, and label printing. Several manufacturers have discovered during a real incident that a licence check phoning home was the thing that stopped the line.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Joint US–Australian OT isolation guidance — reported by SecurityWeek
